title: Array method challenges
idea: Most array methods hand back a new array, one value or a yes or no. Pick the method by the result you need.

analogy.text: A spreadsheet column. A formula fills a new column from each cell, a filter hides rows, and the total at the bottom folds the column into one number.
analogy.breaks: Spreadsheet filters only hide rows; `filter` builds a new, shorter array.

points: `map`, `filter` and `slice` return a new array and leave the original unchanged.
`reduce` folds an array into one value; `find` returns the first match or `undefined`.
`sort` reorders the array in place; `flat` unwraps one level of nesting.

hero.title: A chain, one result at a time

steps.caption: Start with `numbers`. Each method takes an array in and hands a new result on.
`filter` receives the whole array and runs its test once per item.
It returns a new array of the items that passed. `numbers` is unchanged.
Chaining: the new array from `filter` is the input of `map`.
`map` returns an array of the same length, one result per item.
`reduce` also gets a start value, here `0`, and a function that adds one item.
It adds 4, then 8, then 12 to the running total and returns that one value.
The chain ends with a plain number. `numbers` still holds its six items.

code.title: Ten array methods
code.caption: Run it. Change `n > 4` in `find` to `n > 40` and predict the result. Then check `original`.

challenges.intro: Methods like `map` take a small arrow function, such as `(n) => n * 2`; a later lesson explains it. Open a hint when stuck.

items.title: Double every number
items.prompt: Write `doubleAll(nums)`. Return an array with every number multiplied by 2.
hints: You want one result for every item, so the new array has the same length.
`map` calls your function on each item and collects the results in a new array.
Write `nums.map(...)` with an arrow function that returns `n * 2`, and `return` the whole expression.

items.title: Keep the even numbers
items.prompt: Write `keepEvens(nums)`. Return an array with only the even numbers, in their original order.
hints: You want some of the items, so the result may be shorter.
`filter` keeps an item when your function returns `true` for it.
Test `n % 2 === 0`. Avoid `n % 2 === 1`: odd negative numbers leave remainder -1.

items.title: Add up a list
items.prompt: Write `sum(nums)`. Return the total of all the numbers. For an empty array, return `0`.
hints: Many values become one value. That is a job for `reduce`.
`reduce` takes a function `(total, n)` and a start value. Think about what the total is for no numbers.
Return `total + n` from the function, and pass `0` as the second argument of `reduce`.

items.title: Find the first long word
items.prompt: Write `firstLongWord(words)`. Return the first word with 6 or more letters, or `undefined` if no word is that long.
hints: You want one item, not an array of matches.
`find` returns the first item for which your function returns `true`, or `undefined` when none match.
Test `word.length >= 6`. `find` already gives `undefined` when nothing matches.

items.title: Is any number negative?
items.prompt: Write `hasNegative(nums)`. Return `true` if at least one number is below 0, otherwise `false`.
hints: The answer is a yes or no, not a new array.
`some` returns `true` as soon as your function returns `true` for any item.
Use `nums.some(...)` with the test `n < 0`. On an empty array `some` returns `false`.

items.title: Only allowed values
items.prompt: Write `onlyAllowed(items, allowed)`. Return `true` if every item is in the `allowed` array, otherwise `false`. An empty `items` array gives `true`.
hints: Check each item against the list, then ask whether all of them passed.
`every` returns `true` only when your function returns `true` for every item.
Inside `every`, test `allowed.includes(item)`. An empty `items` array gives `true` by itself.

items.title: Take the last items
items.prompt: Write `lastItems(items, n)`. Return a new array with the last `n` items. `n` can be 0 or larger than the array.
hints: A negative start index counts from the end: `slice(-2)` returns the last two items.
Careful: `-0` is just `0`, so `slice(-0)` returns the whole array. Handle `n` of 0 on its own, or compute the start.
Compute the start yourself: `items.length - n`, but never below 0. `Math.max(0, x)` returns the larger of 0 and `x`.

items.title: Sort numbers ascending
items.prompt: Write `sortAscending(nums)`. Return a new array with the numbers from smallest to largest. Do not change the original array.
hints: `sort` compares items as text unless you give it a compare function.
`(a, b) => a - b` puts the smaller number first. `sort` also reorders the array it is called on.
Copy first with spread, then sort the copy: `[...nums].sort(...)`.

items.title: Flatten one level
items.prompt: Write `flattenOnce(list)`. Return a new array where every nested array is opened by one level. Deeper nesting stays as it is.
hints: Opening nested arrays is called flattening. Arrays have a method for it.
`flat(depth)` opens that many levels of nesting. Check what the default depth is.
The default depth is 1, so a plain `list.flat()` is enough.

items.title: Remove duplicates
items.prompt: Write `unique(items)`. Return a new array without duplicates. Keep the first appearance of each item, in the original order.
hints: Keep an item only if it is the first of its kind.
`filter` passes the index as a second argument. `items.indexOf(item)` gives the position of the first match.
Keep the item when `items.indexOf(item) === i`, where `i` is the index `filter` passes in.

pitfalls: A `{ }` arrow body needs `return`; without it `map` fills the array with `undefined`.
Pass a compare function to `sort`; the default order is text, so 10 sorts before 9.
Give `reduce` a start value, or it throws a TypeError on an empty array.

quiz.why: `find` returns one item, or `undefined` when nothing matches. `filter` always returns an array, here an empty one.

takeaway: Chain methods to reshape data, and copy before you `sort`.

starters: How do I choose between map, filter and reduce?
Which array methods change the original array?
